## Overview

Backpressure in a streaming pipeline is the mechanism by which a slow downstream consumer signals an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate, rather than letting an unbounded buffer grow until the process runs out of memory.

Without backpressure, a fast producer can overwhelm a slow consumer by filling buffers until system memory is exhausted, leading to crashes or severe performance degradation. Backpressure prevents this by ensuring the producer respects the consumer's processing capacity.

## Common Implementations

### Bounded Queues with Blocking

The producer writes items to a queue with a fixed size. Once the queue reaches capacity, the producer's send operation blocks until the consumer drains items and space becomes available. This is a simple, synchronous approach commonly used in thread-based systems.

### Credit-Based Flow Control

The consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send a fixed number of items (credits). The producer tracks available credits and sends accordingly. When credits are exhausted, the producer waits until the consumer grants more. This model decouples producer and consumer timing and works well in asynchronous and distributed systems.

### Reactive-Pull Models

Instead of the producer pushing items, the consumer requests items on its own schedule. The producer only emits in response to pull requests. This inverts the flow: demand is explicit and synchronous with consumption, preventing any possibility of buffer overflow.
